# Conti Ransomware Leaks and Public Attribution Record

## Executive assessment

The sources collectively describe Conti as a highly organized ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) enterprise rather than a loose collection of individual hackers. Public reporting portrays a business-like structure in which malware developers, testers, administrators, reverse engineers, penetration testers, negotiators, affiliates, and possibly initial-access brokers contributed to a scalable extortion model. The Conti leaks were significant because they exposed internal conversations, operational planning, recruitment practices, spending decisions, technical development, and apparent relationships with other cybercrime services. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

The strongest public attribution record in the supplied material is divided into two parts. First, Rewards for Justice identifies five online aliases—“Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis”—as malicious cyber actors believed to be linked to Conti and associates them with Russia, Wizard Spider, Conti, and several malware or intrusion tools. This is a government assessment and reward notice, not a judicial finding of guilt. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)) Second, the U.S. Department of Justice identifies Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko as defendants in Conti-related criminal cases. The supplied DOJ record states that the first four were charged in 2023 and that Lytvynenko was charged in 2025 and pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud in 2026. The material does not establish that any of these defendants is one of the five aliases listed by Rewards for Justice. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

My assessment is that the evidence supports a confident conclusion that Conti operated through a commercialized RaaS model and that the 2022 leaks materially exposed its organizational structure. It also supports a careful distinction between public intelligence attribution and court-based attribution: the former names aliases and assesses links to Conti, while the latter identifies defendants and charges or plea information. The supplied sources do not provide enough evidence to merge those two identity sets.

## Sources and evidentiary status

| Source ID | Source | Evidentiary character | Main contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Rewards for Justice, “Conti” | U.S. government reward notice and attribution assessment | Aliases, alleged Russian association, victim and operational figures, associated tools |
| S2 | Rapid7, “Conti Ransomware Group Internal Chats Leaked Over Russia-Ukraine Conflict” | Threat-intelligence analysis | Leaked chat archive, operational practices, technical development, infrastructure, alleged funding and political context |
| S3 | Center for Internet Security, “The Conti Leaks: A Case of Cybercrime’s Commercialization” | Cybersecurity-sector analysis incorporating MS-ISAC observations | Commercial structure, departments, staffing, affiliates, initial-access brokers, SLTT victim reporting |
| S4 | U.S. Department of Justice, “Conti Ransomware” | Official criminal case and victim-information record | Named defendants, charges, plea update, procedural posture, victim count stated by DOJ |

The sources do not have equal legal or analytical status. S4 is the most authoritative source for the existence and procedural posture of the federal cases. S1 is authoritative for what the U.S. government publicly offered as a reward and how it characterized the aliases, but its language is explicitly framed around people “believed to be linked” to Conti. S2 and S3 are analytical sources: they provide important context and interpretation but should not be treated as criminal verdicts.

## Conti as a ransomware-as-a-service operation

### Business model and double extortion

Conti is described as a ransomware-as-a-service group that used double extortion. The model involved obtaining access to victim networks, stealing data, encrypting systems, and threatening to publish or sell the stolen information if the victim did not pay. Conti’s ransom process reportedly directed victims to an online portal to negotiate and complete payment. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); [S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

This model separated the creation and maintenance of the ransomware platform from at least some of the intrusion and extortion activity. CIS explains that RaaS operators can lease malware or services to affiliates, who conduct intrusions and share proceeds with the developers. The article describes a commonly reported revenue division of approximately 70 percent to affiliates and 30 percent to developers, while also emphasizing the role of initial-access brokers that sell already established access to victim environments. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

The commercial structure created several operational advantages. Affiliates could specialize in compromising networks, while the core organization focused on maintaining malware, testing evasion capabilities, negotiating payments, and managing infrastructure. The separation also allowed the core group to scale attacks without personally carrying out every intrusion. CIS’s analysis concludes that affiliates helped operators offload risk and increase the number of potential victims. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

### Scale and victimology

Rewards for Justice states that Conti ransomware was first detected in 2019 and was used in more than 1,000 ransomware operations targeting U.S. and international critical infrastructure. It identifies healthcare networks, law-enforcement agencies, emergency medical services, 9-1-1 dispatch centers, and municipalities among the affected sectors. The same source states that more than 400 organizations worldwide were victimized, including more than 290 in the United States. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The DOJ page gives a different but related figure, stating that Conti affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims in the United States and around the world. These figures should not automatically be treated as irreconcilable. “More than 1,000 ransomware operations” may refer to incidents or campaigns, whereas “more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims” may refer to affected entities. The sources do not define their counting methods sufficiently to determine whether the figures measure the same population. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); [S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

Ransom demands reportedly varied widely, with some reaching as high as $25 million. That figure is presented by Rewards for Justice as part of its description of Conti’s activity; the supplied material does not identify a particular victim or transaction supporting the maximum amount. It should therefore be understood as a reported upper-end demand rather than a verified average or typical payment. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

## What the leaks revealed

### The 2022 disclosure

On February 27, 2022, a Twitter account identified as “@ContiLeaks” released a large collection of internal Conti chat logs after Conti publicly expressed support for the Russian government following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Rapid7 reports that the initial archive, titled `1.tgz`, contained approximately 14 megabytes of chat logs distributed across 393 JSON files. Some messages were encrypted and could not be read, making the dataset incomplete. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The leaked materials reportedly included internal communications, screenshots of tools, discussions of exploits and development processes, usernames and passwords, alleged command-and-control and storage-server access details, and a purported ransomware source-code file. Rapid7 expressly stated that it did not access the remote systems associated with the exposed credentials and recommended against doing so. This limitation is important: the analysis was based on the released material and did not validate every credential, server, or claim contained in the leak. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

### Distinct departments and personnel

The leaks exposed a division of labor resembling a conventional software or technology company. CIS reports that Conti used “Coders” to develop malicious code and integrate technologies, “Testers” to assess ransomware performance against security products, “Administrators,” “Reverse Engineers,” and “Penetration Testers/Hackers.” Spamming functions were reportedly contracted externally. The source states that an insider estimated more than 60 personnel in July 2021, mostly coders and testers, although staffing changed over time and some individuals were dismissed following security incidents. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

The structure indicates that Conti’s capabilities were institutionalized. Technical development, quality assurance, operational administration, reconnaissance, and intrusion-related work were treated as distinct functions. The evidence does not prove that every employee had a formal employment relationship in the conventional legal sense, but it does show a level of specialization inconsistent with the idea of a purely informal criminal collective.

### Product development and security testing

Rapid7 characterizes Conti as operating much like a software company. The chats reportedly discuss feature development, problems encrypting very large files, and efforts to obtain demonstrations of endpoint-detection products so that the ransomware could be modified to evade detection. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

CIS identifies several concrete examples of this product-oriented approach: Conti reportedly allocated $60,000 to obtain a valid Cobalt Strike license, budgeted several thousand dollars per month for security and antivirus software used by testers, and redirected reverse-engineering work toward Windows 11 in July 2021. These reported expenditures suggest deliberate investment in testing, compatibility, reconnaissance, and evasion. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

Rapid7 also reports that Conti used phishing as an initial-access method and that leaked discussions included phishing templates, malicious-document delivery, dynamic-analysis evasion, and command-and-control infrastructure. The supplied evidence therefore depicts an end-to-end operational pipeline: lure or access acquisition, network compromise, malware deployment, data theft, encryption, negotiation, and publication threats. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

## Public attribution and identity records

### Government attribution of aliases

Rewards for Justice offers up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of people who, while acting at the direction or control of a foreign government, participate in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure in violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. The notice identifies “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” as online aliases of malicious cyber actors believed to be linked to Conti. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The same notice associates Conti with Wizard Spider and describes Conti as a Russian government-linked RaaS group. It also lists TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader as associated malicious cyber applications. These are government-published associations, but the language “believed to be linked” signals an intelligence assessment rather than a final judicial determination regarding each alias or tool relationship. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The page lists Russia as an associated location. It also states that after the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Conti operators pledged support to the Russian government and threatened critical-infrastructure organizations in countries perceived to be conducting cyberattacks or war against Russia. Rapid7 separately reports internal political conflict after the statement, including members who sided with Ukraine and a subsequent modification of Conti’s public position. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/); [S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

### DOJ defendants and procedural posture

The DOJ identifies two Conti-related criminal case numbers. Case 3:23-CR-00092 names Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov. The page states that, in September 2023, those defendants were charged with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

Case 3:23-CR-00088 concerns Oleksii Lytvynenko. The DOJ page states that he was charged in November 2025 with conspiracy to deploy Conti ransomware and that he entered a guilty plea to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, on June 10, 2026. The page lists sentencing for September 10, 2026. Because the supplied page itself states that the first four defendants are presumed innocent, allegations against them should not be reported as adjudicated facts. Lytvynenko’s guilty plea establishes a different procedural posture, but the supplied material does not provide the full plea agreement, factual proffer, or sentencing outcome. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

### Limits on alias-to-defendant linkage

No supplied source explicitly states that Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, Zhuykov, or Lytvynenko used the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” or “Dandis.” Accordingly, the public record supplied here supports two parallel attribution layers but not a definitive identity bridge between them:

1. **Intelligence and reward layer:** aliases believed linked to Conti, with Russia and Wizard Spider associations. ([S1](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))
2. **Criminal-case layer:** named defendants charged or, in Lytvynenko’s case, partially adjudicated through a guilty plea. ([S4](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

This distinction is essential for an accurate OSINT report. Treating the aliases as proven identities of the defendants would exceed the evidence supplied.

## Conti’s later fragmentation and continuing threat

Rapid7 observed that Conti took down exposed infrastructure after the chat disclosure but assessed that the group remained active and significant, reporting a resumption of normal operations by March 9, 2022. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

CIS provides a later retrospective assessment: by May 2022, the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into smaller units, while the data-leak and negotiation infrastructure reportedly shut down approximately one month later. This suggests organizational fragmentation rather than the disappearance of personnel, expertise, or affiliated criminal capabilities. However, the supplied sources do not identify every successor group or establish a complete continuity chain. ([S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

## Conclusion

The evidence presents Conti as a commercialized, technically capable RaaS organization built around specialization and scalability. Its internal leaks exposed a structured workforce, budgets, recruitment, testing, malware development, security-evasion efforts, and relationships with affiliates and initial-access brokers. These disclosures substantially strengthened the public understanding of how ransomware operations function as businesses rather than merely as isolated hacking crews. ([S2](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [S3](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

The attribution record is credible but layered. Rewards for Justice publicly associates five aliases with Conti and describes the organization as Russian government-linked, while the DOJ identifies five named defendants in Conti-related prosecutions. The supplied evidence does not directly connect the aliases to the defendants. A responsible conclusion is therefore that the public sources support Conti’s organizational attribution and the existence of Conti-related criminal cases, but they do not support assigning a particular alias to a particular defendant without additional evidence.

infrastructure as a result of the chat disclosure. At that time, we assessed that due to their sophisticated capability, deep funding, and quick recovery from exposed infrastructure in November 2021, they remained an active and significant threat. As of March 9, 2022, our threat intelligence team has observed a resumption of normal operations from Conti. On February 27, Twitter user @ContiLeaks released a trove of chat logs from the ransomware group, Conti – a sophisticated ransomware group whose manual was publicly leaked last year . Ahead of the chat log disclosures, Conti pledged their support for the Russian Government following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. However, a number of members sided with Ukraine, causing strife within the organization. Two days later, Conti posted a second message revising their statement to condemn the war and to strike back only if Russian critical infrastructure is targeted. At the time of the leak, a file titled `1.tgz` was released on the “AnonFiles” website, containing 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files. However, some of the messages were encrypted and could not be read, so the information provided is necessarily incomplete. The remaining files contained internal Conti communications, screenshots of tools, and discussions of their exploits and design processes. On February 28 and March 1, a bevy of additional files were posted, along with a number of pro-Ukraine tweets. Among both sets of leaked messages, there were a number of usernames and passwords for a variety of accounts. Additionally, user @ContiLeaks shared access details for a number of alleged Conti command and control servers, plus storage servers for stolen files. However, we have not accessed any of the data necessitating access to remote servers or the use of usernames and passwords, and we strongly recommend against doing so. @ContiLeaks also shared a file that they purport to be the source code for the Conti ransomware but declined to share the password except with “trusted parties.” @ContiLeaks did, however, name one alleged Conti developer, providing their email address and Github. The scale of the leaked information suggests that the leaker is likely either a very senior member of the group or a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates. Conti is a business – and a well-funded one Much of the discussion within the chat logs concerns fairly mundane things – interviewing potential operators of the group, payment for services, out-of-office messages, gossip, and discussions of products. Based on the leaked chats, the Conti interview process actually looks a lot like a standard technical interview, with coding exercises to be performed hosted on public code repositories, salary negotiations, and the status of ongoing products. In addition to other financial information related to specific actors, the leaked chats have revealed Conti’s primary Bitcoin address, which contains over two billion USD as of February 28, 2022. Moreover, a conversation on April 9, 2021 between “mango” and “johnyboy77” indicates Russian FSB involvement in some portion of their funding and that the FSB were interested in files from the media outlet Bellingcat on “Navalny” – an apparent reference to Alexei Navalny, the currently imprisoned opposition leader in Russia. Conti development Conti seems to operate much like a software company – the chat logs disclose concerns with the development of specific features for targets and a particular difficulty in encrypting very large files. The Conti team also attempted to get demos of popular endpoint detection software with the intent to develop their malware to avoid detection. Two of the actors, “lemur” and “terry” shared phishing templates (included verbatim in Appendix B at the end of this post) to be used against potential targets. Conti gains initial access in many ways, with phishing a popular line of attack due in part to its relatively high efficacy and low cost. Conti often uses phishing emails to establish a presence on targeted networks. A screenshot of the Conti control panel was also leaked, showing a number of compromised hosts and a breakdown of the operating systems, antiviruses, user rights, and detailed information about the infected assets. Further discussions detailed the use of infrastructure against targets, disclosing a number of both known and unknown Conti command and control domains. At the time of this post, only a small number of the previously unknown command and control domains appear to be active. Conversations between two operators, “Stern” and “Bentley” discuss the use of third parties for malicious documents, favoring certain providers over others. They also discuss logistics for how to deliver ransomware without being detected by dynamic analysis. In a conversation between the two back in June of 2021, Stern discloses that Conti wants to start their own cryptocurrency but does not know who to work with. There is no evidence that anything came of this desire, and Conti continues to use Bitcoin for their ransoms. Other groups assert they are strictly business In stark contrast to Conti, other groups have made it clear to the public that despite their “business model,” they take no public stance on this crisis. LockBit is remaining aloof from the conflict and made it clear that they intend to operate as usual. Although it is believed that LockBit is a Russian organization, they assert that “we are all simple and peaceful people, we are all Earthlings,” and “for us it is just business and we are all apolitical.” Another ransomware group, ALPHV, claims to be “extremely saddened” by Conti’s pledge of support and condemns Conti. Their message concludes, “The Internet, and even more so its dark side, is not the place for politics.” Rumors of Conti’s demise have been greatly exaggerated Conti’s payment and “support” portal is still live, even following the infighting and leaks. Conti has repeatedly proven to be one of the most capable ransomware actors and these chats indicate that the group is well-organized and still very well-funded despite the schism. Any suggestion that these leaks spell the end for Conti is overstated, and we expect that Conti will continue to be a powerful player in the ransomware space. What you can do We are keeping an eye on dark web activity related to Conti and other ransomware groups and want to reiterate the following steps for protecting yourself from ransomware: User education, especially related to well-crafted phishing campaigns Asset and vulnerability management, including reducing your external attack surface Multi-factor authentication Additionally, it is worth ensuring that you are well-guarded against the exploits and malware commonly used by Conti (vulnerabilities provided in Appendix A at the end of this post). Furthermore, security teams should also take some time to review CISA’s recent report on the group. For further discussion on how to protect yourself from ransomware, see our ransomware prevention solution . Verizon's DBIR reported that 2021-2022 saw a 13% increase, approximately the same level of growth observed in the last five years combined. Verizon's researchers took a closer look at this trend and unearthed some useful context. First, they found that ransomware had been present in about 70% of malware breaches over the previous year. Approximately two in five ransomware incidents used desktop sharing software and involved a confidentiality compromise with respect to the CIA Triad . Slightly fewer (35%) leveraged email as an attack vector. What's Behind The Rise in Ransomware? An important cause of ransomware's growth is the shift towards commercialization of cybercrime. Indeed, many of the most prolific cybercriminal groups have undergone significant changes in operations to scale efforts and expand revenue. In several instances, public reporting has shown these groups incorporating divisions previously associated with legitimate corporations including HR departments with recruiters, finance and accounting, as well as negotiators to coordinate ransom payment. Beyond these structures, likely the most significant trend has been the shift to Ransomware as a Service (RaaS), which has seen groups lease out malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers (often in a 70-30 split). The below graphic depicts the RaaS relationship and the part that initial access brokers (IABs) play in greater detail. Source: Alan Liska, Ransomware: Understand. Prevent. Recover. Several sources of evidence point to cybercrime's growing commercialization but none as explicitly as the recent Conti leaks. Let’s examine what insights it offered below. Overview of Conti RaaS Conti was a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion to pressure victims into paying up. It also appears to have had ties to other malware outfits, most notably TrickBot . Conti ransom note template (Source: Bleeping Computer ) Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, the Conti operators announced their "full support" for Russia. Just a few days following this commitment, a Twitter account dubbed " Contileaks " dumped an archive of chat messages taken from Conti's internal communications dating back to the beginning of 2021, as reported by KrebsonSecurity . It also published additional internal chats from 2020. In the months that followed, Conti's handlers began dismantling their operations. In May 2022 , Bleeping Computer wrote that the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, gaining even greater mobility (and evasion from law enforcement) for its members. It was about a month after that when the RaaS operation shut down its data leaks and negotiation infrastructure. Findings of the Conti Leaks The Conti leaks have provided several important insights into how a major RaaS group carries out its operations. These include how Conti ran its "office" and how it worked to improve its "product." Distinct Employees with Distinct Goals In the second part of his investigation on the Conti leaks, KrebsonSecurity revealed that Conti's handlers divided their operations into several business units and brought on staff with specific skill sets. For example, it hired programmers as "Coders" to write malicious code and integrate different technologies, while it relied on "Testers" to validate how the ransomware payload performed against security technologies. The operation also had "Administrators," "Reverse Engineers," and "Penetration Testers/Hackers" working internally, with spamming functions contracted outside the organization. Each of those departments had its own budget, though business units were able to borrow funds from one another. According to a Conti insider, the gang employed more than 60 people – mostly Coders and Testers – in July 2021. That number didn't remain consistent, however, as the group sometimes let people go following internal security breaches. Streamlined Operations to Improve Their 'Product' The third installment of KrebsonSecurity's analysis revealed that the Conti gang took several steps to improve its "product" on an ongoing basis. These initiatives included the following: Allocating $60,000 to acquire a valid license for the Cobalt Strike network penetration testing and reconnaissance tool. Budgeting several thousand dollars each month to pay for security and antivirus software that the "Testers" could use for their evaluations. Redefining the focus of the "Reverse Engineers" in July 2021 to concentrate on Windows 11, Microsoft's newest operating system at the time. The MS-ISAC Perspective on the Conti Leaks To get more insight into the Conti leaks, we sat down with the Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) team at the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC). Here's what they had to say. How does commercialization help malicious actors like Conti's operators? Organized ransomware groups operating in a corporate structure allow cybercriminals to conduct highly impactful attacks at scale. For example, instead of expending time and resources on gaining initial access to a victim’s environment, a ransomware group can outsource this work by purchasing already established access from IABs. As a result, ransomware affiliates tasked with conducting attacks are able to increase their number of victims, creating a more dangerous cyber threat landscape for network defenders. Operating through affiliates offers several benefits to the RaaS operator. Principally, because they're not conducting intrusions themselves, they're able to offload risk and dramatically increase the number of potential targets, as there's theoretically no limit to the number of affiliates who can carry out these intrusions. This allows the developers to focus efforts and capital on developing and retooling their software, thereby reinvesting in the enterprise. Has the MS-ISAC seen evidence of cybercrime's commercialization in the daily work of supporting members? If so, what has this looked like? Yes, the MS-ISAC regularly receives reporting about SLTT ransomware attacks involving sophisticated RaaS groups like Conti. From mid-2020 through January 2022, for instance, 22 Conti-related SLTT ransomware attacks were reported to the MS-ISAC, impacting organizations ranging from municipal governments to education facilities. Open-source reporting indicates that the “Conti group” is also tied to the Ryuk ransomware variant, which impacted an additional 89 SLTT government entities from late 2018 through mid-2021. To this day, other RaaS groups continue to attack SLTT governments, including at least 23 ransomware attacks associated with the LockBit 2.0 variant since August 2021. Where does cybercrime's commercialization put an emphasis for the future? I would say it only increases the victim set. Ultimately, there's no silver bullet against ransomware. But SLTTs can still do their best to have their bases covered and put themselves in the best position to prevent and react to breaches when they occur. That means becoming members of the MS-ISAC so they can receive our products, leverage our resources, and deploy appropriate protections. For our team, we need to watch closely for shifts in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that could catch members by surprise, and we need to provide the timely intelligence and guidance that will help them proactively defend their networks. If threat actors evolve, we need to, as well. This also includes things like bolstering partnerships that allow us to share timely intel with members. The Center for Internet Security and the MS-ISAC understand the formidable threat RaaS groups present to SLTTs. They offer services and resources to help organizations better defend themselves. These include no-cost services like Malicious Domain Blocking and Reporting (MDBR), which prevents IT systems from connecting to harmful web domains and thereby helps to limit infections related to known malware, ransomware, phishing, and other cyber threats. A robust ransomware defense should also involve some form of endpoint security solution such as the CIS Endpoint Security Services (ESS), which is available to SLTTs through a partnership with CrowdStrike. Finally, the threat underscores the importance for SLTTs to implement the cybersecurity best practices found in the CIS Critical Security Controls , which are designed to prevent all types of cyber attacks. Defending Against Ransomware Like Conti The CTI team's thoughts on the Conti leaks point to an important truth about ransomware. Certainly, some attackers have taken it upon themselves in recent years to restructure as RaaS operations and commercialize their business functions. But for all its innovations, ransomware's aims have not fundamentally changed as a threat. Its purpose still revolves around denying access to files by encrypting infected machines. Subsequently, MS-ISAC members can use the solutions identified by the CTI team along with these resources to strengthen their defenses against ransomware going forward. Malicious cyber actors known by their online aliases of “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” are believed to be linked to the Conti ransomware group. Conti (also known as Wizard Spider), is a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group that has targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. After Russian military forces invaded neighboring Ukraine in February 2022, Conti ransomware operators pledged support to the Russian government and threatened critical infrastructure organizations of countries perceived to carry out cyberattacks or war against the Russian government. First detected in 2019, Conti ransomware has been used to conduct more than 1,000 ransomware operations targeting U.S. and international critical infrastructure, such as law enforcement agencies, emergency medical services, 9-1-1 dispatch centers, and municipalities. These healthcare and first responder networks are among the more than 400 organizations worldwide victimized by Conti, over 290 of which are located in the United States. Conti operators typically steal victims’ files and encrypt the servers and workstations in an effort to force a ransom payment from the victim. The ransom letter instructs victims to contact the actors through an online portal to complete the transaction. If the ransom is not paid, the stolen data is sold or published to a public site controlled by the Conti actors. Ransom amounts vary widely, with some ransom demands being as high as $25 million. As of March 9, 2022, our threat intelligence team has observed a resumption of normal operations from Conti. On February 27, Twitter user @ContiLeaks released a trove of chat logs from the ransomware group, Conti – a sophisticated ransomware group whose manual was publicly leaked last year . Ahead of the chat log disclosures, Conti pledged their support for the Russian Government following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. However, a number of members sided with Ukraine, causing strife within the organization. Two days later, Conti posted a second message revising their statement to condemn the war and to strike back only if Russian critical infrastructure is targeted. At the time of the leak, a file titled `1.tgz` was released on the “AnonFiles” website, containing 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files. However, some of the messages were encrypted and could not be read, so the information provided is necessarily incomplete. The remaining files contained internal Conti communications, screenshots of tools, and discussions of their exploits and design processes. On February 28 and March 1, a bevy of additional files were posted, along with a number of pro-Ukraine tweets. Among both sets of leaked messages, there were a number of usernames and passwords for a variety of accounts. Additionally, user @ContiLeaks shared access details for a number of alleged Conti command and control servers, plus storage servers for stolen files. However, we have not accessed any of the data necessitating access to remote servers or the use of usernames and passwords, and we strongly recommend against doing so. @ContiLeaks also shared a file that they purport to be the source code for the Conti ransomware but declined to share the password except with “trusted parties.” @ContiLeaks did, however, name one alleged Conti developer, providing their email address and Github. The scale of the leaked information suggests that the leaker is likely either a very senior member of the group or a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates. Conti is a business – and a well-funded one Much of the discussion within the chat logs concerns fairly mundane things – interviewing potential operators of the group, payment for services, out-of-office messages, gossip, and discussions of products. Based on the leaked chats, the Conti interview process actually looks a lot like a standard technical interview, with coding exercises to be performed hosted on public code repositories, salary negotiations, and the status of ongoing products. In addition to other financial information related to specific actors, the leaked chats have revealed Conti’s primary Bitcoin address, which contains over two billion USD as of February 28, 2022. Moreover, a conversation on April 9, 2021 between “mango” and “johnyboy77” indicates Russian FSB involvement in some portion of their funding and that the FSB were interested in files from the media outlet Bellingcat on “Navalny” – an apparent reference to Alexei Navalny, the currently imprisoned opposition leader in Russia. Conti development Conti seems to operate much like a software company – the chat logs disclose concerns with the development of specific features for targets and a particular difficulty in encrypting very large files. The Conti team also attempted to get demos of popular endpoint detection software with the intent to develop their malware to avoid detection. Two of the actors, “lemur” and “terry” shared phishing templates (included verbatim in Appendix B at the end of this post) to be used against potential targets. Conti gains initial access in many ways, with phishing a popular line of attack due in part to its relatively high efficacy and low cost. Conti often uses phishing emails to establish a presence on targeted networks. A screenshot of the Conti control panel was also leaked, showing a number of compromised hosts and a breakdown of the operating systems, antiviruses, user rights, and detailed information about the infected assets. Further discussions detailed the use of infrastructure against targets, disclosing a number of both known and unknown Conti command and control domains. At the time of this post, only a small number of the previously unknown command and control domains appear to be active. Conversations between two operators, “Stern” and “Bentley” discuss the use of third parties for malicious documents, favoring certain providers over others. They also discuss logistics for how to deliver ransomware without being detected by dynamic analysis. In a conversation between the two back in June of 2021, Stern discloses that Conti wants to start their own cryptocurrency but does not know who to work with. There is no evidence that anything came of this desire, and Conti continues to use Bitcoin for their ransoms. Other groups assert they are strictly business In stark contrast to Conti, other groups have made it clear to the public that despite their “business model,” they take no public stance on this crisis. LockBit is remaining aloof from the conflict and made it clear that they intend to operate as usual. Although it is believed that LockBit is a Russian organization, they assert that “we are all simple and peaceful people, we are all Earthlings,” and “for us it is just business and we are all apolitical.” Another ransomware group, ALPHV, claims to be “extremely saddened” by Conti’s pledge of support and condemns Conti. Their message concludes, “The Internet, and even more so its dark side, is not the place for politics.” Rumors of Conti’s demise have been greatly exaggerated Conti’s payment and “support” portal is still live, even following the infighting and leaks. Conti has repeatedly proven to be one of the most capable ransomware actors and these chats indicate that the group is well-organized and still very well-funded despite the schism. Any suggestion that these leaks spell the end for Conti is overstated, and we expect that Conti will continue to be a powerful player in the ransomware space. What you can do We are keeping an eye on dark web activity related to Conti and other ransomware groups and want to reiterate the following steps for protecting yourself from ransomware: User education, especially related to well-crafted phishing campaigns Asset and vulnerability management, including reducing your external attack surface Multi-factor authentication Additionally, it is worth ensuring that you are well-guarded against the exploits and malware commonly used by Conti (vulnerabilities provided in Appendix A at the end of this post). Furthermore, security teams should also take some time to review CISA’s recent report on the group. For further discussion on how to protect yourself from ransomware, see our ransomware prevention solution . Verizon's DBIR reported that 2021-2022 saw a 13% increase, approximately the same level of growth observed in the last five years combined. Verizon's researchers took a closer look at this trend and unearthed some useful context. First, they found that ransomware had been present in about 70% of malware breaches over the previous year. Approximately two in five ransomware incidents used desktop sharing software and involved a confidentiality compromise with respect to the CIA Triad . Slightly fewer (35%) leveraged email as an attack vector. What's Behind The Rise in Ransomware? An important cause of ransomware's growth is the shift towards commercialization of cybercrime. Indeed, many of the most prolific cybercriminal groups have undergone significant changes in operations to scale efforts and expand revenue. In several instances, public reporting has shown these groups incorporating divisions previously associated with legitimate corporations including HR departments with recruiters, finance and accounting, as well as negotiators to coordinate ransom payment. Beyond these structures, likely the most significant trend has been the shift to Ransomware as a Service (RaaS), which has seen groups lease out malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers (often in a 70-30 split). The below graphic depicts the RaaS relationship and the part that initial access brokers (IABs) play in greater detail. Source: Alan Liska, Ransomware: Understand. Prevent. Recover. Several sources of evidence point to cybercrime's growing commercialization but none as explicitly as the recent Conti leaks. Let’s examine what insights it offered below. Overview of Conti RaaS Conti was a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion to pressure victims into paying up. It also appears to have had ties to other malware outfits, most notably TrickBot . Conti ransom note template (Source: Bleeping Computer ) Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, the Conti operators announced their "full support" for Russia. Just a few days following this commitment, a Twitter account dubbed " Contileaks " dumped an archive of chat messages taken from Conti's internal communications dating back to the beginning of 2021, as reported by KrebsonSecurity . It also published additional internal chats from 2020. In the months that followed, Conti's handlers began dismantling their operations. In May 2022 , Bleeping Computer wrote that the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, gaining even greater mobility (and evasion from law enforcement) for its members. It was about a month after that when the RaaS operation shut down its data leaks and negotiation infrastructure. Findings of the Conti Leaks The Conti leaks have provided several important insights into how a major RaaS group carries out its operations. These include how Conti ran its "office" and how it worked to improve its "product." Distinct Employees with Distinct Goals In the second part of his investigation on the Conti leaks, KrebsonSecurity revealed that Conti's handlers divided their operations into several business units and brought on staff with specific skill sets. For example, it hired programmers as "Coders" to write malicious code and integrate different technologies, while it relied on "Testers" to validate how the ransomware payload performed against security technologies. The operation also had "Administrators," "Reverse Engineers," and "Penetration Testers/Hackers" working internally, with spamming functions contracted outside the organization. Each of those departments had its own budget, though business units were able to borrow funds from one another. According to a Conti insider, the gang employed more than 60 people – mostly Coders and Testers – in July 2021. That number didn't remain consistent, however, as the group sometimes let people go following internal security breaches. Streamlined Operations to Improve Their 'Product' The third installment of KrebsonSecurity's analysis revealed that the Conti gang took several steps to improve its "product" on an ongoing basis. These initiatives included the following: Allocating $60,000 to acquire a valid license for the Cobalt Strike network penetration testing and reconnaissance tool. Budgeting several thousand dollars each month to pay for security and antivirus software that the "Testers" could use for their evaluations. Redefining the focus of the "Reverse Engineers" in July 2021 to concentrate on Windows 11, Microsoft's newest operating system at the time. The MS-ISAC Perspective on the Conti Leaks To get more insight into the Conti leaks, we sat down with the Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) team at the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC). Here's what they had to say. How does commercialization help malicious actors like Conti's operators? Organized ransomware groups operating in a corporate structure allow cybercriminals to conduct highly impactful attacks at scale. For example, instead of expending time and resources on gaining initial access to a victim’s environment, a ransomware group can outsource this work by purchasing already established access from IABs. As a result, ransomware affiliates tasked with conducting attacks are able to increase their number of victims, creating a more dangerous cyber threat landscape for network defenders. Operating through affiliates offers several benefits to the RaaS operator. Principally, because they're not conducting intrusions themselves, they're able to offload risk and dramatically increase the number of potential targets, as there's theoretically no limit to the number of affiliates who can carry out these intrusions. This allows the developers to focus efforts and capital on developing and retooling their software, thereby reinvesting in the enterprise. Has the MS-ISAC seen evidence of cybercrime's commercialization in the daily work of supporting members? If so, what has this looked like? Yes, the MS-ISAC regularly receives reporting about SLTT ransomware attacks involving sophisticated RaaS groups like Conti. From mid-2020 through January 2022, for instance, 22 Conti-related SLTT ransomware attacks were reported to the MS-ISAC, impacting organizations ranging from municipal governments to education facilities. Open-source reporting indicates that the “Conti group” is also tied to the Ryuk ransomware variant, which impacted an additional 89 SLTT government entities from late 2018 through mid-2021. To this day, other RaaS groups continue to attack SLTT governments, including at least 23 ransomware attacks associated with the LockBit 2.0 variant since August 2021. Where does cybercrime's commercialization put an emphasis for the future? I would say it only increases the victim set. Ultimately, there's no silver bullet against ransomware. But SLTTs can still do their best to have their bases covered and put themselves in the best position to prevent and react to breaches when they occur. That means becoming members of the MS-ISAC so they can receive our products, leverage our resources, and deploy appropriate protections. For our team, we need to watch closely for shifts in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that could catch members by surprise, and we need to provide the timely intelligence and guidance that will help them proactively defend their networks. If threat actors evolve, we need to, as well. This also includes things like bolstering partnerships that allow us to share timely intel with members. The Center for Internet Security and the MS-ISAC understand the formidable threat RaaS groups present to SLTTs. They offer services and resources to help organizations better defend themselves. These include no-cost services like Malicious Domain Blocking and Reporting (MDBR), which prevents IT systems from connecting to harmful web domains and thereby helps to limit infections related to known malware, ransomware, phishing, and other cyber threats. A robust ransomware defense should also involve some form of endpoint security solution such as the CIS Endpoint Security Services (ESS), which is available to SLTTs through a partnership with CrowdStrike. Finally, the threat underscores the importance for SLTTs to implement the cybersecurity best practices found in the CIS Critical Security Controls , which are designed to prevent all types of cyber attacks. Defending Against Ransomware Like Conti The CTI team's thoughts on the Conti leaks point to an important truth about ransomware. Certainly, some attackers have taken it upon themselves in recent years to restructure as RaaS operations and commercialize their business functions. But for all its innovations, ransomware's aims have not fundamentally changed as a threat. Its purpose still revolves around denying access to files by encrypting infected machines. Subsequently, MS-ISAC members can use the solutions identified by the CTI team along with these resources to strengthen their defenses against ransomware going forward.
